items.q: What happens to a star like the Sun at the end of its life?
items.correct: It swells into a red giant, then sheds its layers to leave a white dwarf.
items.misconception: It explodes as a supernova and becomes a black hole.
items.random_wrong: It simply switches off like a bulb.
items.why: Only massive stars end as supernovae or black holes. Low-mass stars like the Sun become red giants, then white dwarfs.

items.q: What stops a stable main-sequence star from collapsing?
items.correct: Outward pressure from fusion balances the inward pull of gravity.
items.misconception: There is no gravity inside a star, so nothing makes it collapse.
items.random_wrong: The star is solid, so it holds its shape.
items.why: A star is a balance of forces: gravity pulls inwards, radiation pressure from fusion pushes outwards. When fuel runs low the balance is lost.

items.q: What does the Big Bang theory describe?
items.correct: The universe began from a single point and has been expanding ever since.
items.misconception: An explosion of matter into empty, pre-existing space.
items.random_wrong: The moment the Sun first formed.
items.why: It describes the expansion of space itself from a hot, dense start — supported by red-shift and the cosmic microwave background.
